latin.2618: XXXVI. Praeter Remonstrantes autem, ex Reformatis qui subscribunt Synodo Dordracenae nonnulli quoque gratiam distinguunt in sufficientem atque efficacem, sensu tamen non parum diverso. Quippe hac distinctione utitur Paulus Testardus, dum viveret Pastor Ecclesiae Blaesensis, in Irenico thesi trecentesima, & in libro de Natura & Gratia pluribus in locis. Sed per gratiam sufficientem intelligit illam ipsam quam universalem vocat, per gratiam autem efficacem, eam quam nominat particularem.
latin.2619: XXXVII. Itaque, ex ejus mente, gratia ista sufficiens non est gratia aliqua subjectiva, quae hominem intus disponat ad fidem & resipiscentiam: sed tantum gratia quaedam objectiva, quae in eo consistit quod salus homini possibilis redditur, tum per Christi satisfactionem, quae sustulit obstaculum illud quod justitia divina opponebat, ne homines peccatorum veniam impetrarent: tum per externam Dei vocationem, & invitationem ad fidem & resipiscentiam, sive per verbum praedicationis, sive per opera naturae & providentiae.
latin.2620: XXXVIII. Gratiam autem illam dicit esse sufficientem, quoniam dat homini posse servari si velit: adeo ut si homo salutis particeps non fiat, stet tantum penes ejus pravitatem & malignitatem, neque de Deo queri possit, quasi aliquid ipsi denegaverit, sine quo absolute non possit esse salvus: cum habeat objectum in sufficienti lumine propositum, & mentem & voluntatem, quae per se possint & debeant illud amplecti atque suscipere: ac quominus id fiat, obstet sola ejus perversitas, cujus ipse causa est, ac propter quam nullam habet rationem de Deo querendi.
latin.2621: XXXIX. Agnoscit tamen ille nunquam contingere posse ut, si non aliud accedat, aliquis per solam istam sufficientem gratiam salvetur: idque propter nativam hominis pravitatem atque improbitatem, quae impedit ne bene utatur mediis illis a Deo propositis, & alioquin in se ad salutem sufficientibus. Et sic fidem & resipiscentiam, ad quas homo sufficienter facultatibus Physicis instructus est, moraliter illi impossibilem reddit. Unde emergit necessitas particularis alicujus gratiae, quae pravitatem hominis corrigat, & ita mentem atque voluntatem intus disponat atque afficiat, ut excussis pravis habitibus, salutem extrinsecus oblatam amplectatur, & fide atque resipiscentia ad misericordiam divinam confugiat, quam gratiam particularem ideo vocat efficacem.
latin.2622: XL. Verum alii Reformati gratiae distinctionem in sufficientem atque efficacem communiter repudiant. Quippe censent nullam gratiam revera sufficientem esse & dici posse, quae etiam non sit efficax. Idque quia ut homo reapse convertatur, requiritur tale Dei auxilium, quo non simpliciter ad bonum moveatur & alliciatur, sed quo voluntas ejus flectatur & determinetur, ut bonum velit & illi adhaereat, absque quo nunquam foret, ut eo ferretur voluntas, obstante ingenita hominis pravitate.
latin.2623: XLI. Etenim communis est Reformatorum omnium, qui Dordracenam Synodum sequuntur, sententia, gratiam Dei, cui tribuenda est hominis conversio, & omnia quae eam subsequuntur bona opera, esse efficacem per se, nec ejus efficaciam ullo modo pendere a cooperatione, sive consensu voluntatis humanae, cum causa sit infallibilis istius consensus, sive cooperationis. Idque congruenter decretis istius Synodi. Siquidem in rejectione errorum circa tertium & quartum articulum Canone 8. damnat eos qui docent Deum in hominis regeneratione eas suae omnipotentiae vires non adhibere, quibus voluntatem ejus ad fidem & conversionem potenter & infallibiliter flectat: sed positis omnibus gratiae operationibus, quibus Deus ad hominem convertendum utitur, hominem tamen Deo, & spiritui regenerationem ejus intendenti, & regenerare ipsum volenti, ita posse resistere, & actu ipso saepe resistere, ut sui regenerationem prorsus impediat, adeoque in ipsius manere potestate, ut regeneretur, vel non regeneretur. Canone vero nono damnat eos quoque qui docent, Gratiam & liberum arbitrium esse causas partiales simul concurrentes ad conversionis initium; nec gratiam ordine causalitatis, efficientiam voluntatis antecedere: Id est, Deum non prius hominis voluntatem efficaciter juvare ad conversionem, quam voluntas ipsa hominis se moveat ac determinet.
latin.2624: XLII. Quomodo autem Deus in Electis veram conversionem operetur, sic explicat eadem Synodus, Non tantum, inquit, evangelium illis externe praedicari curat, & mentem eorum per Spiritum Sanctum potenter illuminat, ut recte intelligant & dijudicent quae sunt Spiritus Dei; sed ejusdem etiam spiritus regenerantis efficacia ad intima hominis penetrat, cor clausum aperit, durum emollit, praeputiatum circumcidit, voluntati novas qualitates infundit, facitque eam ex mortua vivam, ex mala bonam, ex nolente volentem, ex refractaria morigeram, agitque & roborat eam, ut ceu arbor bona fructus bonarum actionum proferre possit. In capite doctrinae de hominis corruptione & conversione, ejusque modo articulo undecimo.
latin.2625: XLIII. Articulo vero sequenti addit eam Dei operationem esse plane supernaturalem, potentissimam simul & suavissimam, mirabilem, arcanam & ineffabilem, virtute sua nec creatione, nec mortuorum resuscitatione minorem aut inferiorem: adeo ut omnes illi, in quorum cordibus admirando hoc modo Deus operatur, certo, infallibiliter & efficaciter regenerentur, & actu credant.
latin.2626: XLIV. Proinde cum illa Dei operatio in iis sese non exerat qui reipsa non credunt & poenitentiam agunt, idcirco qui isti Synodo subscribunt Theologi, negant illis gratiam sufficientem dari, quantumcunque externa verbi praedicatione ad poenitentiam & fidem invitentur, & quibusdam etiam internis Spiritus Sancti motibus percellantur.
latin.2627: XLV. Est enim observandum Reformatos qui negant omnes eos qui non convertuntur gratiam ad conversionem sufficientem habere, non negare tamen quin aliquousque gratia Dei operetur in multis qui sese in peccatis obfirmant, nec ad Deum per fidem & resipiscentiam accedunt. Sunt enim, ex eorum mente, quaedam ad conversionem sive regenerationem praevia, quae communia sunt Electis & reprobis, & virtute verbi spiritusque, tam in horum quam in illorum cordibus excitantur. Qualia sunt notitia voluntatis divinae, sensus peccati, timor poenae, cogitatio de liberatione, spes aliqua veniae, aliique motus similes.
latin.2628: XLVI. Fatentur multos, quos Deus eo modo vocat ad fidem & conversionem, nolle Deum vocantem sequi, & Spiritui Sancto quae ad salutem eorum faciunt suggerenti resistere, ac tandem motus illos per verbum & Spiritum Sanctum in iis excitatos penitus extinguere, & sic propria culpa in aeternum perire.
latin.2629: XLVII. Haec est inter alios Theologorum Britannorum doctrina, actis Synodi Dordrechtanae inserta. Exponentes enim suam sententiam de articulis tertio & quarto, & agentes de iis quae ad conversionem sunt antecedanea, sic ea de re statuunt thesi secunda & sequentibus, Sunt quaedam effecta interna ad conversionem, sive regenerationem praevia, quae virtute verbi, spiritusque in nondum justificatorum cordibus excitantur; qualia sunt notitia voluntatis divinae, sensus peccati, timor poenae, cogitatio de liberatione, spes aliqua veniae. Quos Deus mediante verbo per spiritum suum hunc in modum afficit, eos ad fidem conversionemque vere, & serio vocat & invitat. Quos ita afficit Deus non deserit nec desistit in vera ad conversionem via promovere, priusquam ab illis per neglectionem voluntariam, aut hujus gratiae initialis repulsam, deseratur.
latin.2630: XLVIII. Hi praecedanei effectus, virtute verbi spiritusque in hominum mentibus producti, rebellis voluntatis vitio, suffocari ac penitus extingui possunt, & in multis solent; adeo ut nonnulli in quorum mentibus virtute verbi spiritusque impressa fuit aliqualis notitia veritatis divinae, aliqualis dolor de peccatis suis, aliquod desiderium & aliqua cura liberationis, mutentur plane in contrarium, veritatem rejiciant & odio habeant, concupiscentiis suis se tradant, in peccatis occalleant, & absque desiderio vel cura liberationis in iisdem computrescant.
latin.2631: XLIX. Addunt ne electos quidem ipsos in hisce praecedaneis ad regenerationem actibus ita se gerere unquam, quin propter negligentiam & resistentiam suam possint juste a Deo deseri & derelinqui: sed eam esse erga illos specialem Dei misericordiam, ut quamvis hanc gratiam excitantem & illuminantem repellant aliquamdiu, aut suffocent, eos tamen iterum, iterumque urgeat Deus, nec desistat promovere, donec eosdem gratiae suae prorsus subjugaverit, ac in statu filiorum regeneratorum collocaverit.

sections.title: Testard: sufficient grace as universal, efficacious as particular
sections.pass_a: XXXVI. But besides the Remonstrants, of the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort some also distinguish grace into sufficient and efficacious, yet in a sense not a little different. For Paulus Testardus, while he lived Pastor of the Church of Blois, uses this distinction, in the Irenicum thesis three hundred, & in the book on Nature & Grace in several places. But by sufficient grace he understands that very grace which he calls universal, but by efficacious grace, that which he names particular.
pass_b: Thesis XXXVI. Apart from the Remonstrants, some of the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort also divide grace into sufficient and efficacious, though in a quite different sense. Paulus Testardus, pastor of the church at Blois in his lifetime, uses this distinction in his Irenicum, thesis 300, and in many places in his book on nature and grace.
By sufficient grace, however, he means what he calls universal grace, and by efficacious grace what he names particular grace.

sections.title: Testard: sufficient grace is objective, not subjective
sections.pass_a: XXXVII. And so, in his mind, that sufficient grace is not some subjective grace, which disposes man inwardly to faith & repentance: but only a certain objective grace, which consists in this that salvation is made possible for man, both through the satisfaction of Christ, which removed that obstacle which divine justice opposed, lest men should obtain pardon of sins: and through the external calling of God, & invitation to faith & repentance, whether through the word of preaching, or through the works of nature & providence.
pass_b: Thesis XXXVII. In his view, then, this sufficient grace is not a subjective grace that inwardly disposes a person to faith and repentance. It is only an objective grace, which consists in salvation being made possible for a person.

This happens in two ways: through Christ's satisfaction, which took away the barrier that divine justice set against people obtaining forgiveness of sins, and through God's outward call and invitation to faith and repentance, given either by the preached word or by the works of nature and providence.

sections.title: Why Testard calls this grace sufficient
sections.pass_a: XXXVIII. But he says that grace is sufficient, because it gives man to be able to be saved if he will: so that if man does not become partaker of salvation, it rests only with his depravity & malignity, nor can he complain of God, as if he had denied him something, without which he absolutely could not be saved: since he has the object set forth in sufficient light, & a mind & will, which of themselves can & ought to embrace and receive it: and that this does not happen, only his perversity stands in the way, of which he himself is the cause, and on account of which he has no ground for complaining of God.
pass_b: Thesis XXXVIII. He calls that grace sufficient because it gives a person the ability to be saved if he wills. So if someone does not come to share in salvation, the cause lies only in his own depravity and malice, and he cannot complain of God as though God had denied him something without which he simply could not be saved.

For he has the object set before him in sufficient light, and he has a mind and will that of themselves can and should embrace and accept it. Only his own perversity, of which he himself is the cause, prevents this, and for that reason he has no ground to complain of God.

sections.title: Testard: why particular, efficacious grace is needed
sections.pass_a: XXXIX. Yet he acknowledges that it can never happen that, if nothing else is added, anyone is saved through that sufficient grace alone: and that because of the native depravity and wickedness of man, which hinders him from using well those means set forth by God, & otherwise in themselves sufficient for salvation. And thus it renders faith & repentance, for which man is sufficiently equipped with Physical faculties, morally impossible for him. Whence emerges the necessity of some particular grace, which may correct the depravity of man, & so dispose and affect the mind and will inwardly, that, depraved habits being shaken off, it may embrace the salvation offered from without, & by faith and repentance flee to the divine mercy, which particular grace he therefore calls efficacious.
pass_b: Thesis XXXIX. He admits, though, that unless something more is added, no one can ever be saved by this sufficient grace alone. The reason is man's inborn depravity and wickedness, which keeps him from making good use of the means God sets before him, means otherwise sufficient for salvation in themselves.

So that depravity makes faith and repentance morally impossible for him, although his physical faculties equip him adequately for them. Hence the need for a particular grace to correct man's depravity and so to dispose and move his mind and will from within that, once his corrupt habits are shaken off, he embraces the salvation offered from outside and takes refuge in God's mercy by faith and repentance. This particular grace Testard therefore calls efficacious.

sections.title: Other Reformed reject the division
sections.pass_a: XL. But other Reformed commonly repudiate the distinction of grace into sufficient and efficacious. For they judge that no grace truly is sufficient & can be called so, which is not also efficacious. And that because for man to be really converted, such help of God is required, by which he is not simply moved & allured to good, but by which his will is bent & determined, to will the good & cleave to it, without which it would never be, that the will would be carried thither, the inborn depravity of man standing in the way.
pass_b: Thesis XL. Other Reformed theologians, however, generally reject the distinction of grace into sufficient and efficacious. In their judgment no grace is really sufficient, or can be called so, unless it is also efficacious.

Their reason is that for a person to be actually converted, God must give a help that does more than simply move and draw him toward the good: it must bend and determine his will to will the good and hold to it. Without such help the will would never be carried there, since man's inborn depravity blocks the way.

sections.title: Dort: grace efficacious of itself (rejection of errors 8 and 9)
sections.pass_a: XLI. For the opinion common to all the Reformed, who follow the Synod of Dort, is that the grace of God, to which is to be attributed the conversion of man, & all the good works which follow it, is efficacious of itself, nor does its efficacy in any way depend on the cooperation, or consent of the human will, since it is the cause of that infallible consent, or cooperation. And that in agreement with the decrees of that Synod. For in the rejection of errors on the third & fourth article Canon 8. it condemns those who teach that God in the regeneration of man does not apply those powers of his omnipotence, by which he may powerfully & infallibly bend his will to faith & conversion: but that, all the operations of grace being posited, which God uses for converting man, man yet can so resist God, & the spirit intending his regeneration, & willing to regenerate him, & in very act often resists, that he wholly hinders his own regeneration, and so it remains in his own power, to be regenerated, or not to be regenerated. But in the ninth Canon it condemns those also who teach, That grace & free choice are partial causes concurring together to the beginning of conversion; and that grace in the order of causality, does not precede the efficiency of the will: That is, that God does not efficaciously help the will of man to conversion, before the will of man itself moves & determines itself.
pass_b: Thesis XLI. All the Reformed who follow the Synod of Dort hold in common that the grace of God, to which man's conversion and all the good works that follow it must be credited, is efficacious of itself. Its efficacy in no way depends on the cooperation or consent of the human will, since grace itself causes that infallible consent or cooperation.

This agrees with the decrees of that Synod. In the rejection of errors on the third and fourth articles, canon 8, it condemns those who teach 'that in regenerating a person God does not use those powers of his omnipotence by which he would bend the person's will to faith and conversion with power and without fail; but that, with every working of grace that God uses for converting a person in place, the person can still resist God and the Spirit who intends and wills to regenerate him, and often actually does, so as to prevent his own regeneration entirely, and so it remains in his own power whether he is regenerated or not.'

In canon 9 it also condemns those who teach 'that grace and free choice are partial causes acting together at the start of conversion, and that grace does not come before the will's own working in the order of causes'; that is, 'that God does not effectively help a person's will toward conversion before that will moves and determines itself.'

sections.title: Dort: how God works true conversion in the elect (article 11)
sections.pass_a: XLII. But how God works true conversion in the Elect, the same Synod explains thus, Not only, it says, does he take care that the gospel be preached to them externally, & powerfully illuminates their mind by the Holy Spirit, that they may rightly understand & discern the things which are of the Spirit of God; but by the efficacy of the same regenerating spirit he also penetrates to the inmost parts of man, opens the closed heart, softens the hard, circumcises the uncircumcised, infuses new qualities into the will, and makes it from dead living, from bad good, from unwilling willing, from refractory compliant, and moves & strengthens it, that like a good tree it may be able to bring forth fruits of good actions. In the head of doctrine on the corruption of man & conversion, and its manner article eleven.
pass_b: Thesis XLII. The same Synod explains how God works true conversion in the elect: 'He not only has the gospel preached to them outwardly and powerfully enlightens their minds by the Holy Spirit, so that they rightly understand and judge the things of the Spirit of God.

By the power of the same regenerating Spirit he also reaches into the innermost being of a person: he opens the closed heart, softens the hard one, circumcises the uncircumcised, and pours new qualities into the will. He makes the will alive where it was dead, good where it was bad, willing where it was unwilling, obedient where it was stubborn, and he moves and strengthens it so that, like a good tree, it can bear the fruit of good actions.' This is in the head of doctrine on man's corruption and conversion and its manner, article 11.

sections.pass_a: XLIII. But in the following article it adds that this operation of God is plainly supernatural, at once most powerful & most sweet, wonderful, secret & ineffable, in its power neither less nor inferior to creation, nor to the raising of the dead: so that all those, in whose hearts God works in this admirable manner, are certainly, infallibly & efficaciously regenerated, & actually believe.
pass_b: Thesis XLIII. In the next article the Synod adds that this working of God is wholly supernatural, both most powerful and most gentle, wonderful, hidden and beyond words, and no less in power than creation or the raising of the dead. So all in whose hearts God works in this wonderful way are regenerated surely, infallibly and effectively, and actually believe.

sections.title: Hence no sufficient grace for those who do not believe
sections.pass_a: XLIV. Accordingly since that operation of God does not exert itself in those who in fact do not believe & repent, therefore the Theologians who subscribe to that Synod, deny that sufficient grace is given to them, however much they are invited to repentance & faith by the external preaching of the word, & are struck also by certain internal motions of the Holy Spirit.
pass_b: Thesis XLIV. Since that working of God does not show itself in those who do not actually believe and repent, the theologians who subscribe to that Synod deny that such people are given sufficient grace, however much the outward preaching of the word invites them to repentance and faith, and even though some inward motions of the Holy Spirit stir them.

sections.title: Yet grace works to some degree in the unconverted
sections.pass_a: XLV. For it is to be observed that the Reformed who deny that all those who are not converted have grace sufficient for conversion, do not however deny that the grace of God works to some extent in many who harden themselves in sins, and do not come to God through faith & repentance. For there are, in their mind, certain things preliminary to conversion or regeneration, which are common to the Elect & the reprobate, & by the power of the word and spirit, are excited in the hearts both of these and of those. Such are knowledge of the divine will, sense of sin, fear of punishment, thought of deliverance, some hope of pardon, and other like motions.
pass_b: Thesis XLV. Note that the Reformed who deny that everyone who is not converted has grace sufficient for conversion do not deny that God's grace works to some degree in many who harden themselves in their sins and do not come to God by faith and repentance.

In their view there are certain things that go before conversion or regeneration, common to the elect and the reprobate, which the power of the word and Spirit rouses in the hearts of both alike: knowledge of God's will, a sense of sin, fear of punishment, thoughts of deliverance, some hope of pardon, and other motions of that kind.

sections.title: Many resist and perish by their own fault
sections.pass_a: XLVI. They confess that many, whom God calls in that way to faith & conversion, will not follow God calling, & resist the Holy Spirit suggesting the things which make for their salvation, and at last wholly extinguish those motions excited in them through the word & the Holy Spirit, & so perish eternally by their own fault.
pass_b: Thesis XLVI. They admit that many whom God calls to faith and conversion in this way refuse to follow God's call, resist the Holy Spirit as he prompts them toward what makes for their salvation, and in the end entirely stifle the motions that the word and the Holy Spirit stirred in them, and so are lost for ever through their own fault.

sections.title: The British theologians at Dort on preliminary effects
sections.pass_a: XLVII. This is among others the doctrine of the British Theologians, inserted in the acts of the Synod of Dort. For setting out their opinion on the third & fourth articles, & treating of those things which are antecedent to conversion, they lay down thus on that matter in the second thesis & those following, There are certain internal effects preliminary to conversion, or regeneration, which by the power of the word, and of the spirit are excited in the hearts of those not yet justified; such as are knowledge of the divine will, sense of sin, fear of punishment, thought of deliverance, some hope of pardon. Those whom God by means of the word through his spirit affects in this manner, he truly, & seriously calls & invites to faith and conversion. Those whom God so affects he does not desert nor cease to advance in the true way to conversion, before he is deserted by them through voluntary neglect, or rejection of this initial grace.
pass_b: Thesis XLVII. Among others, this is the teaching of the British theologians, included in the Acts of the Synod of Dort. Setting out their opinion on the third and fourth articles and dealing with what comes before conversion, they state in their second thesis and those that follow:

'There are certain inward effects that go before conversion or regeneration, which the power of the word and the Spirit rouses in the hearts of people not yet justified, such as knowledge of God's will, a sense of sin, fear of punishment, thoughts of deliverance, and some hope of pardon. Those whom God moves in this way by his Spirit, through the word, he calls and invites to faith and conversion truly and in earnest.
Those whom God so moves he does not abandon, nor does he stop leading them forward on the true road to conversion, until they abandon him by wilful neglect or by refusing this initial grace.'

sections.title: The British theologians: preliminary effects can be stifled
sections.pass_a: XLVIII. These preceding effects, produced in the minds of men by the power of the word and spirit, can be suffocated and wholly extinguished by the vice of the rebellious will, & in many are wont to be; so that some in whose minds by the power of the word and spirit was impressed some knowledge of divine truth, some sorrow for their sins, some desire & some care of deliverance, are changed plainly into the contrary, reject the truth & hold it in hatred, give themselves up to their lusts, grow callous in sins, & without desire or care of deliverance rot away in them.
pass_b: Thesis XLVIII. 'These preliminary effects, produced in people's minds by the power of the word and Spirit, can be smothered and entirely put out through the fault of a rebellious will, and in many they usually are.

So some people, in whose minds the power of the word and Spirit has stamped a measure of knowledge of divine truth, some grief for their sins, and some longing and concern for deliverance, are turned completely the other way: they reject the truth and hate it, hand themselves over to their desires, grow hardened in their sins, and rot in them with no longing or concern for deliverance.'

sections.title: The British theologians: God's special mercy toward the elect
sections.pass_a: XLIX. They add that not even the elect themselves ever so conduct themselves in these preceding acts toward regeneration, but that on account of their negligence & resistance they could justly be deserted & forsaken by God: but that such is the special mercy of God toward them, that although they repel this exciting & illuminating grace for some while, or suffocate it, God yet urges them again, and again, nor ceases to advance them, until he has wholly subjugated them to his grace, and placed them in the state of regenerate sons.
pass_b: Thesis XLIX. They add that even the elect never behave in these acts that go before regeneration so well that God could not justly abandon and forsake them for their negligence and resistance.

But God's special mercy toward them is such that, though they push away or smother this stirring and enlightening grace for a time, he presses them again and again and does not stop leading them forward until he has brought them wholly under his grace and set them in the state of regenerate children.
